articles.title: Two powerful federal courts face push to break free from DC bubble as unlikely duo steps in
articles.summary: Sens. Chris Coons and Ashley Moody introduced the Better Bench Act to drop the D.C. residency requirement for Court of Federal Claims judges.
articles.body: A bipartisan team of senators is proposing legislation that they say will broaden the pool of qualified judges available to serve on two powerful federal courts with nationwide jurisdiction. Sens. Chris Coons, D-Delaware, and Ashley Moody, R-Florida, introduced a bill on Tuesday that would remove the requirement that judges sitting on the Court of Federal Claims and the Federal Circuit live within 50 miles of Washington, D.C. Both courts have nationwide jurisdiction, though their specialized dockets differ. The Court of Federal Claims primarily handles claims against the federal government, while the Federal Circuit hears appeals involving patents, trademarks, government contracts and other areas. A decision from either court, for example, could affect Coons’ constituents in Delaware or Moody’s in Florida. The claims court hears arguments from entities seeking money or other relief from the federal government whereas the circuit court, which is a feeder for Supreme Court justices, reviews decisions from lower courts and agencies in relation to the federal government. MIKE DAVIS: FEDERAL COURT SETS DANGEROUS PRECEDENT AGAINST 99-YEAR-OLD JUDGE "Americans deserve the best, most qualified judges, especially in areas like intellectual property law where expertise is key to understanding complex cases and fairly deciding the future of many entrepreneurs’ businesses," Coons said of the legislation. "For too long, we have limited the pool of judges available to take on the toughest IP and federal contract cases to those willing to uproot their lives and move to Washington, D.C. No longer. This bipartisan bill ensures that courts of national jurisdiction can draw from a pool of national talent." Legal scholars who spoke with Fox News Digital saw merit in the senators' proposal. "It's often difficult to recruit top-level talent from across the country to relocate to the District of Columbia for these judgeships," Heritage Foundation senior legal fellow Zach Smith told Fox News Digital, noting that the Court of International Trade in New York City has a similarly broad geographic jurisdiction and lacks a residency requirement for judges. "Many other circuit courts of appeal cover multiple states and often the judges on those courts sit throughout the states that that court covers and then they often come together to meet and hear cases and hear oral arguments in a specific location. This type of geographic dispersal it's not an unusual arrangement." Thomas Berry, the director of the libertarian-aligned Cato Institute's Center for Constitutional Studies largely agreed. ‘UNPRECEDENTED’: JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES "These courts have jurisdiction based on the issue involved, so potentially if this meant that the judges were able not just to live elsewhere, but even hear oral arguments elsewhere, that could potentially be more convenient for some types of cases if they're, say, involved parties on the opposite side of the country," Berry told Fox News Digital. Critics may argue that the proposed legislation could increase travel costs to taxpayers by requiring frequent travel for judges to and from D.C. Legal experts may also feel that the ability of judges to regularly meet face to face could lead to a loss of judicial collegiality. Berry noted that some studies show that, during the Coronavirus pandemic, court decisions saw less dissents as judges spent less time in person with one another, but qualified possible concerns by stating that "all of the other regional courts of appeals have been basically working under such a system for over 100 years, and clearly it hasn't gotten in the way from them doing the work that they're meant to do." SUPREME COURT CHIEF JUSTICE PINPOINTS WHAT AMERICANS MISUNDERSTAND ABOUT HIM AND HIS COLLEAGUES Neither expert felt that travel costs would be an issue in implementing this proposal. "For a court that covers the entire country, we should be considering nominating judges from everywhere in America based on merit — not their proximity to the D.C. bubble," Moody, herself a former Florida circuit judge and federal prosecutor, said of the legislation. "My Better Bench Act removes an outdated residency requirement to expand the pool of qualified Americans who can serve and allows our courts to be a better reflection of the nation as a whole." articles.title: She grew up under Soviet rule. Now EU's top diplomat warns Europe against giving Russia what it wants
articles.summary: Kaja Kallas says Russia's sabotage and intimidation campaign aims to weaken European support for Ukraine, warning the strategy will escalate if it works.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Russia is trying to scare Europe into backing off its defense in the region, claims European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who warns it will only lead to Moscow becoming more aggressive if it succeeds. "Their goal is to intimidate us from not supporting Ukraine, from refraining to support them and pressuring Russia," Kallas told Fox News Digital in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly. "What is important for us is that we are not afraid," she continued. "Because otherwise this kind of intimidation actually pays off, and then we will see more of it across the world." For Kallas, Russia’s attempts to intimidate its European neighbors carry a history that reaches well beyond the war in Ukraine. Her mother, Kristi, was just six months old in 1949 when Soviet authorities deported her — along with her mother and her grandmother — to Siberia during Stalin’s mass deportations from the Baltic states. Kallas’ maternal grandfather was separately sent to a Siberian prison camp. Kallas has recounted how her mother was transported east in a cattle car, with fellow deportees drying the infant’s diapers against their own bodies during the freezing journey. The family spent roughly a decade in Siberia before they were allowed to return to Soviet-occupied Estonia in 1959. Kallas was born in Tallinn in 1977 and spent the first 14 years of her life under Soviet rule. Estonia restored its independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union collapsed. FRONTLINE NATO ALLY SHARES SHOCKING TAKE ON RUSSIAN INVASION THREAT Her family would go on to become deeply entwined with the new democratic Estonia. Her father, Siim Kallas, became the first president of the Bank of Estonia after gaining its independence, later serving as foreign minister and prime minister before moving to Brussels as a European commissioner. Kaja Kallas followed her own path from lawyer to member of Estonia’s parliament and then the European Parliament. In 2021, she became Estonia’s first female prime minister and three years later was chosen as the European Union’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy. It was a historic moment — putting a politician who grew up under Soviet occupation at the center of Europe’s response to Russian aggression on the continent. That history has made Kallas one of Europe’s most prominent voices on Moscow — even as officials in her native Estonia and elsewhere along NATO’s eastern flank now caution against interpreting Russia’s recent provocations as preparations for a conventional invasion. Russia invaded Ukraine more than four-and-a-half years ago and shows no signs of backing off despite repeated promises that negotiations for an end of war are ongoing. Asked whether she agreed with Estonian and other Baltic officials who say they do not currently see Russia preparing for such an attack, Kallas instead pointed to Moscow’s growing use of sabotage and the importance of deterrence. "We see that Russia is actually increasing their sabotage acts in Europe," Kallas said. "But of course how far they will go depends very much on us and whether we are investing enough in defense so that it acts as a deterrent." The debate comes as NATO countries confront a string of Russian aircraft and drone incursions, along with suspected sabotage and other hybrid activity across Europe. The incidents have fueled warnings in some European capitals that Moscow is probing the alliance for weaknesses, while officials closer to Russia have cautioned against equating those provocations with preparations for an invasion. US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Fox News Digital in a separate interview this week that his country's intelligence services see no indication Russia is preparing for a full-scale attack on NATO. "We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic states, Poland, but we don’t see it," Tsahkna said. "Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia, we don’t see any change." Kallas, however, argued that Moscow's actions are designed to weaken Western support for Ukraine rather than simply test NATO's defenses. "Their goal is to intimidate us from not supporting Ukraine, from refraining to support them and pressuring Russia," she said. The pressure campaign comes as Washington continues its push for a negotiated end to the war. Kallas said Moscow has yet to demonstrate that it is serious about reaching one. "They should start with stopping bombing the civilians," she said, pointing to recent Russian attacks on Kyiv. "If they are serious about this, they should agree to a ceasefire, sit down at the negotiation table and talk to the Ukrainians." Kallas said Ukraine has already agreed to an unconditional ceasefire while "Russia is just playing games," arguing that coordinated pressure from Washington and its European allies could change Moscow's calculations. articles.title: Republicans fear two key Senate races are slipping from their grasp
articles.summary: Some Republicans are growing worried that two key Senate races once considered critical to holding their majority are slipping from their grasp.
articles.body:
Some Republicans are growing worried that two key Senate races once considered critical to holding their majority are slipping from their grasp.

In more than a dozen interviews with campaign officials, senators and operatives, there is recognition that North Carolina and Georgia are looking less competitive than the party once anticipated and that decisions need to be made soon about whether to keep investing, even as party officials insist they are not walking away from their candidates there.

Republican senators like North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis, said it was time for the party to make some tough decisions about spending.

"You spend the money where we get Republicans elected," Tillis said. "I want them to do that now. I mean you don't spend the money just because you want to help somebody."

Both Rep. Mike Collins, who is trying to unseat Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, and Michael Whatley, who is running against former Gov. Roy Cooper to replace Tillis, are behind in polls and facing questions about their campaigns. A GOP loss in North Carolina – a state President Donald Trump won three times – would give Democrats one of the four flips they need to retake the Senate.

One GOP super PAC, Old North Action, trimmed its ad reservations in North Carolina by about a third last week, one of the clearest signs yet that the party may be losing confidence in the race. Whatley said this week he feels "very comfortable" he will have the money he needs.

"I don't know what the path is for Michael. I mean, I'll just say that. Unless Cooper just completely stumbles," a North Carolina Republican strategist, speaking on the condition of anonymity to freely discuss the political environment, told CNN.

Collins' campaign recently made clear to allies it needs more help in Georgia. In a memo posted on his website and dated Monday, the campaign argued that 1 in 10 voters are "still up for grabs" for Collins. The campaign said they are mostly voters who supported Trump in 2024 and are backing Rick Jackson for governor, who is in a closer race with Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms.

"They should be voting for Mike Collins, and they are not yet, mainly because they do not have a firm opinion of him," the memo says, suggesting stepped-up ad spending could change that.

But the party and its allies are having to spend big to shore up even redder seats, including an investment of well over $100 million in Texas.

"We are erecting a big wall around all of our candidates," Senate Majority Leader John Thune said. "There are headwinds we are facing in all the races around the country."

Party leaders are sending signals that they're still committed to Georgia and North Carolina in particular. Thune headlined a fundraiser for Collins on Thursday night in Atlanta along with Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp. And Trump and Vice President JD Vance each visited North Carolina recently as part of their first stops for candidates following the GOP midterm convention.

A spokesman for the NRSC, Nick Puglia, criticized Ossoff and Cooper in a statement for this story and promised Republicans "will continue working to expose their far-left records to permanently retire them."

NRSC Chairman Sen. Tim Scott pushed back Thursday against any suggestion the committee was deprioritizing Georgia and North Carolina. "Hogwash!" Scott wrote on X .

His denial came after a closed-door meeting with Senate Republicans where he discussed the Senate map. An NRSC spokesperson said Scott spoke positively about Collins and Whatley, saying they were chipping away at their polling deficits.

A crisis of confidence – and some blame for Trump

But confidence is waning in other corners of the GOP.

Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who hosted a fundraiser Monday for a group of Senate GOP candidates in other states, questioned the party's decision to keep plowing money into races that may no longer be winnable.

"Here we are, what, 40 days out? And so I don't think there is a lot that can be done," Cornyn said. "I think it is going to be a matter of where the resources should be deployed."

Cornyn's fundraiser, which he headlined with former President George W. Bush, sent a clear message about his view of the map. The guest list included incumbents and nominees from Alaska, Ohio, Michigan, Iowa, New Hampshire and Minnesota. Collins and Whatley were not there. Notably, Cornyn also excluded GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general who defeated him in a primary this year after getting a late Trump endorsement.

He said he focused his fundraiser on the other states "because I think the money will go a lot further in those places."

Cornyn said he did not think there was anything Whatley could do to turn around his campaign at this point.

"I think if Thom Tillis was on the ticket, things would look a lot different, but the president basically went after him, and now we've got somebody who is not as well-known and he's struggling," Cornyn said.

Whatley painted an optimistic picture of his campaign during a recent radio interview where he was asked about outside funding.

"We certainly do need the groups, you know, like the Republican Party, to come in and be supportive … because the Democratic Party is going to send hundreds of millions of dollars into North Carolina," Whatley said on Thursday. "But I feel very comfortable we are going to have the resources that we need over the next 42 days to prosecute this campaign and win."

Still, when speaking with CNN, several GOP operatives in North Carolina questioned Whatley's campaign strategy in this current environment, noting ads and campaign events supporting the former North Carolina GOP and RNC chair have predominately focused on crime. Meanwhile Cooper, a two-term governor who has never lost a race, has centered his campaign around affordability and economic issues.

"I thought the crime stuff would be effective, that some of the bad stuff he did in office would come back to bite Cooper. It should be a really good message. But, for whatever reason, it's not landing yet," said the GOP strategist. "But they aren't doing anything else. Even when the president came, he mostly harped on crime. It's not resonating, we should be doing something else."

Outside of Old North Action, Republican groups have mostly maintained their ad reservations for the final weeks of the races and the NRSC, the Senate GOP's campaign arm, has already spent $7.9 million in coordinated spending in North Carolina and $3.6 million in Georgia through the end of August.

The optimistic case for Republicans is that North Carolina has a reputation for deciding late. Trump focused heavily on the state in the closing days of the 2024 election, raising speculation that he was concerned about it. He went on to win by 3 percentage points.

"These polls look really rough," the North Carolina GOP strategist said of this year's Senate race. "The good thing is, Republicans always outperform polls. But, never to this degree."

Cooper's campaign, meanwhile, has long urged Democrats against growing complacent in the state. They were especially outspoken after a Supreme Court ruling lifted limits on coordinated spending with political parties, giving the Republican National Committee – which Whatley previously led – more flexibility to spend in races.

"A Democrat has not won statewide federal office here in nearly two decades," Cooper campaign manager Jeff Allen told CNN in a statement. "Whatley's elite DC connections mean Republicans are going to spend whatever it takes to keep this seat."

In Georgia, Collins is confronting a stronger-than-expected incumbent in Ossoff, who is already generating buzz as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. (Ossoff has said he has "zero interest.")

Thune told CNN, shortly before his trip to Atlanta, that he still believes Collins can win.

"I think part of it is, it's a big state, an expensive state and … we've got a House member running, who it just takes a lot of money to get known," Thune said. "I think once you get the name ID up there, you can litigate the contrast."

"It's like every place else," Thune added. "It's a resource issue."

Thune's fundraiser for Collins, which also featured Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, brought in over $400,000 for the candidate, according to a source familiar with the event.

Like Cooper, Ossoff is also wary of Democrats declaring victory too soon. He told CNN earlier this week that he is "taking nothing for granted."

"We're still seeing significant Republican super PAC activity," Ossoff told CNN. "As for the national groups and whatnot, again, every day I run like I am behind."

CNN's Manu Raju contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump’s Greenland deal shadows Xi visit after years of Beijing eyeing Arctic influence
articles.summary: Trump's Greenland security deal blocked China's Arctic ambitions days before Xi Jinping arrived for a state dinner with America's top AI executives.
articles.body: President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington this week, one day after signing a Greenland security agreement that, once in force, would bar non-NATO states such as China from establishing a military presence there, sharpening the Arctic-security backdrop to their face-to-face talks. Xi’s three-day state visit unfolded against that backdrop, with Trump hosting a formal White House arrival ceremony, holding high-stakes talks, joining Xi for a tour of the National Archives and presiding over a state dinner attended by some of America’s most prominent technology executives. A senior U.S. official told Fox News Digital that Trump and Xi discussed the economy, trade, "Super Intelligence" and cooperation on a range of shared priorities, though it remained unclear what concrete agreements emerged from behind closed doors. TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING Trump has so far stopped short of announcing a concrete agreement from Xi’s Washington visit, a contrast to his May trip to Beijing. Trump was already telling reporters before leaving China that the two countries had made "some fantastic trade deals," even though the White House did not release its full economic deal package until two days after the summit. Thursday’s state dinner drew 134 guests, including the two leaders and prominent technology figures such as Jensen Huang of Nvidia, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Lisa Su of AMD, Tim Cook of Apple, Sam Altman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sundar Pichai of Google. Christine Balling, senior vice president for professional affiliations at The Institute of World Politics, told Fox News Digital that inviting America’s top AI tycoons to Thursday night’s state dinner was a strategic move to show Xi that the United States is the world’s top dog in the AI race. 'RED CARPET FOR A DESPOT': TRUMP'S LAVISH XI WELCOME COLLIDES WITH GOP ANTI-COMMUNISM MESSAGE "I think the significance of the timing of this meeting, whether it's intentional or not, shows that the Trump administration is taking The future of AI and the world very, very seriously," she said. "I think that is the most significant takeaway. But the bottom line is, I think the most important images were those of all of the AI techs who were invited to that state dinner." Greenland has emerged as a backdrop to Trump’s two meetings with Xi this year. Negotiations over an expanded U.S. security role there began months before Trump traveled to Beijing in May, while Trump renewed his public pressure over Greenland during the summer as his administration continued negotiations aimed in part at limiting Russian and Chinese influence in the Arctic. Five days before Xi arrived in Washington, Trump announced a Greenland security agreement that was formally signed Sept. 22 and, once in force, would expand the U.S. military position while restricting Chinese military presence and certain sensitive investments in the territory. China has had its eye on Greenland for years, especially as it looks to expand its role in the Arctic. Beijing has shown interest in Greenland’s infrastructure and natural resources, including its valuable rare earth and critical mineral deposits. U.S. officials have also pointed to past Chinese efforts involving a former U.S. naval base and airport projects as signs of Beijing’s broader ambitions in the region. Balling is an expert in foreign policy, particularly in the Western hemisphere, and says Trump’s historic deal with Greenland struck a massive blow to China. TRUMP DECLARES VICTORY IN HISTORIC DEAL WITH GREENLAND AS HE SECURES 'PERMANENT' US MILITARY RIGHTS "Number one, that is a tremendous victory for the United States and frankly, the free world," she said. "It means that the United States has the ability to establish two more bases at present. So we have a Space Force base … and now secured land, air, and sea rights across Greenland. We have the ability to screen out any other country who expresses interest in either establishing any sort of military presence and or investment." "That means that the United States and NATO allies are going to have first right of refusal when it comes to mining, and not only for rare elements, but also oil and gas and data centers." SECURITY EXPERT HAILS TRUMP'S GREENLAND PACT AS A 'BIG DEAL' ON PAR WITH ALASKA PURCHASE China has long sought a larger Arctic role, declaring itself a "near-Arctic state" and promoting a "Polar Silk Road" encompassing commerce, research and resource development. Balling argued that Beijing had reason to oppose the U.S.-Denmark-Greenland agreement because the United States remains heavily reliant on China for several critical-mineral supply chains. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I also have to say for all of those who were mocking the Trump administration and President Trump's talk about buying or invading Greenland, they have an egg on their faces now," she said. "I never for a moment thought that President Trump was serious about this. I think that what he was serious about, was exactly what was achieved in the agreement that was just signed."

articles.title: Lula prohíbe las apuestas deportivas y los casinos online: "Esto es como un cáncer"
articles.summary: Brasil ha dado un giro histórico con la prohibición de las apuestas deportivas y los casinos online. El presidente Lula da Silva firmó este viernes una medida provisional que prohíbe las llamadas 'bets' y su publicidad en todo el país. Los sitios y aplicaciones dejarán de operar el 6 de octubre, mientras que el Congreso tendrá un plazo máximo de 120 días para decidir si mantiene definitivamente la medida.
articles.body: Brasil ha dado un giro histórico con la prohibición de las apuestas deportivas y los casinos online. El presidente Lula da Silva firmó este viernes una medida provisional que prohíbe las llamadas 'bets' y su publicidad en todo el país. Los sitios y aplicaciones dejarán de operar el 6 de octubre, mientras que el Congreso tendrá un plazo máximo de 120 días para decidir si mantiene definitivamente la medida. Lula justificó la decisión por el impacto social de las apuestas, especialmente entre las familias con menos recursos. "No vamos a permitir que utilicen su tarjeta de crédito o las bets para gastar el dinero de la leche de sus hijos, el dinero del pan o el dinero de la comida", afirmó. El Gobierno brasileño sostiene que el fenómeno se ha convertido también en un problema de salud pública y de endeudamiento familiar. La decisión tendrá además un fuerte impacto en el fútbol brasileño. Las casas de apuestas destinan más de 1.000 millones de reales al año en patrocinios de los clubes de la primera división masculina. Los equipos ya habían advertido del agujero económico que podía provocar la prohibición y algunos llegaron a calificar el escenario como "el fin del fútbol". El propio Lula respondió a este argumento poniendo como ejemplo la historia del fútbol brasileño. Reconocido hincha del Corinthians, recordó que él mismo aportó 1.013 reales a una colecta de aficionados para ayudar al club a pagar su deuda. "No pueden decirme que sin las bets los equipos se acaban", afirmó. También recordó los títulos mundiales conquistados por Santos, Flamengo, Internacional, Grêmio, São Paulo y Corinthians antes de la expansión de las apuestas online. La medida abre ahora un periodo de incertidumbre para los clubes que dependen de estos patrocinios. El Gobierno ha anunciado también medidas para facilitar la renegociación de deudas de las familias y ha planteado mecanismos de apoyo al fútbol ante la pérdida de ingresos.

articles.title: Some lawmakers doubt a Congress that’s ‘barely capable of email’ can regulate AI
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — Amid warnings that artificial intelligence could soon wipe out humanity, some lawmakers are not confident that Congress has the expertise or ability to regulate AI.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Amid warnings that artificial intelligence could soon wipe out humanity, some lawmakers are not confident that Congress has the expertise or ability to regulate AI. “A lot of them can’t spell it,” quipped Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. “They just don’t have the experience.” Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., was equally skeptical. “They still don’t know how to get on the internet,” let alone understand AI, he said. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., who represents parts of Silicon Valley, argued that many members of Congress are just not up to speed on AI, and some seem uninterested. “The problem in Congress is not that we don’t have enough computer scientists. It’s that we don’t have enough people who have a basic understanding of how the technology works or are using it,” Khanna said in an interview with NBC News. “It’s like talking about making the rules for driving the road. You don’t have to be an auto mechanic, but it would be nice if you at least were a passenger in a car or had driven a car,” he continued. “And we’ve had a lot of members of Congress who’ve not been passengers in a car when it comes to AI, or certainly haven’t driven it.” One thing that everyone seems to agree on: Congress is not close to regulating AI. Capitol Hill has been notoriously slow to regulate new technology. It hasn’t passed any sweeping, comprehensive legislation regulating the internet, invented more than 40 years ago, instead taking a more piecemeal approach and relying on existing laws. And exactly 20 years after Facebook became available to the public, lawmakers are still struggling to figure out how to regulate social media. New rules aimed at protecting kids online are popular in theory, but actual legislation remains stalled, with House and Senate negotiators deadlocked on the issue. “This is the United States Congress you’re talking about. I mean, nothing moves very quickly,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former astronaut and Navy combat pilot who backs AI regulation. It’s “much easier” to fly a fighter jet than to pass AI legislation, he added. But while there are plenty of skeptics who believe Congress doesn’t have the capability to tackle AI regulations, there are optimists who think it does. One is Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., who is pursuing a master’s degree in machine learning at George Mason University to keep pace with new technology. Beyer served on the bipartisan House Task Force on Artificial Intelligence and now serves on a Democratic commission on AI. “Oh, I very much think there’s a capacity here. Yeah, you don’t need to be a Ph.D. or a master’s in computer science to know what to do next,” said Beyer, who is 76. “I think the parallel is we don’t have to be biologists or chemists to set up the FDA, or lawyers or stockbrokers to set up the SEC. There are 12 to 20 members of Congress already, just in the House, that have AI bills.” What’s blocking any significant legislative movement on AI is political will from Republicans, he argued. “I think we definitely have the capacity. What we need is a speaker who will let us put the bills on the floor,” said Beyer, who has been advocating for Democratic leaders to create a select committee on artificial intelligence if the party wins control of the House this fall. Democrats, a handful of Republicans and key tech leaders believe that Congress needs to step in now and regulate the AI industry following high-profile AI breaches. “AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that … cause a billion deaths,” Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said in an interview with Kristen Welker that will air Sunday on NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he added. President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will host an AI summit with tech leaders in Washington on Tuesday, according to a White House official and a source familiar with the plans. But, given their past comments, it’s likely to focus more on tech innovation and competition than on reining in the companies. Trump has repeatedly said that he does not want to “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” as he put it in a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly this week. “We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” Trump said. He has also dismissed the recent apocalyptic warnings as a “hoax” and said regulations will impede America in its race with China for AI dominance. Johnson has said some safety guardrails are needed but has argued Congress should not get in the way of American innovation. At a recent campaign rally, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who is running in one of the most competitive Senate races in November and is mentioned as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, blamed Trump and the “weakness of our politics” for congressional inaction on AI. “Tech titans dig bunkers while warning us the new intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction. Congress debates youth sports, and the president builds a ballroom,” Ossoff said. “An ancient establishment, barely capable of email, sleepwalks into a technological revolution, while the president dismantles precautions and calls us fools for worrying.” The House made a big push on AI in 2024, with a bipartisan task force that held two dozen hearings and produced a 273-page report on a framework for potential AI legislation, with nearly 90 recommendations. Many of those recommendations have been translated into bills that are now being considered by committees and subcommittees, said Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., who chaired the task force and holds a master’s degree in AI from UCLA. One of these measures is the Frontier Act, his bipartisan bill with Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., that would create national safety rules for building and using advanced AI models. “Would I prefer that the process had moved faster? Yes, absolutely,” Obernolte said. “Has it been moving as fast as it could, given the constraints that everyone was under? Yes, I believe it has.” Obernolte said the bipartisan AI task force was not renewed this Congress because it had issued its report and fulfilled its mission. But he said it has created a group of AI experts on Capitol Hill whom other lawmakers can rely on and ask questions of. The task force, he said, began with members who knew nothing about AI and are now “deeply educated” on the issue. Asked if he’s confident Congress can rise to the occasion and pass something on AI, Obernolte replied: “Confident is too strong, but hopeful.” Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, was more pessimistic, pointing out that the Senate this month failed to pass a landmark cryptocurrency bill despite years of bipartisan work, and that AI developments seem to be moving at warp speed. “This process of legislating takes so long that by the time we even got to that step — I mean, crypto, we’re four years in. We haven’t passed it,” Moreno said. “So imagine AI four years in. We’re dealing with stuff that’s not even relevant in four years.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who serves on the Judiciary and Homeland Security committees, said he doesn’t believe most members of Congress have the expertise to understand all of the complexities of AI, but nor should they focus on trying to regulate every aspect of the technology. Instead, he said, lawmakers should focus on passing legislation, like his AI LEAD Act, that would hold tech companies legally liable for any harm caused by AI. “Expertise? No, but we … don’t need to set minute regulations. What we should do is, for example, we should open the courthouse doors so that citizens who are harmed by AI, who when AI agents go out and crash the banking system or commit cyberattacks or hack data, the companies should be liable for that,” Hawley said.

articles.title: Wave of overlooked 'left-wing' lawsuits could come with an unexpected price tag for Americans
articles.summary: A report from Power The Future and the Heritage Foundation warns climate lawsuits could cost American households nearly $1,465 more per year.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: American households could end up paying $1,465 more per year on average in energy costs if "anti-energy" climate lawsuits against oil and gas companies are successful, according to a new report first obtained by Fox News Digital. Americans will "pay a lot more" if the far-left "get their way," warned Heritage Foundation chief economist E.J Antoni, who co-authored the report with Power The Future founder Daniel Turner. Hundreds of lawsuits and other state-level "climate superfund" laws could increase the cost of gasoline, electricity and other everyday necessities Americans rely on, the report estimates. SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA The new analysis, obtained by Fox News Digital, comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear a closely-watched lawsuit next month out of Boulder, Colorado, which could drastically shape the future of climate litigation. "If those folks on the radical left wing who are anti-energy, if they get their way, your costs are going to go up," Antoni told Fox News Digital. "Your household is going to pay a lot more. The energy is going to get much more expensive." "You may think it's bad now, but it will get significantly worse," he added. The report estimates energy companies could face an additional $194 billion in annual costs, which the authors argue would ultimately be passed on to consumers through higher prices rather than absorbed entirely by companies or their shareholders. Those costs could add roughly 41 cents to a gallon of gasoline and increase residential electricity rates by about 8.6%, according to the analysis. "Every single time a company is sued, yes, they pay some damages, but ultimately they will just charge people more for their product to recoup those losses," Turner told Fox News Digital. LAWSUITS COST EVERY AMERICAN HOUSEHOLD THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS. SUPREME COURT CAN HELP The report examined more than 300 pending lawsuits, three state "climate superfund" laws, 12 state legislative proposals and one federal bill. Its estimate reflects a "full-success scenario" in which all of those measures prevail; it does not predict that they will. The analysis counted each lawsuit only once and excluded duplicate filings. In fact, Antoni said the estimate may be conservative because some lawsuits do not specify the damages they are seeking, leaving potential court awards open-ended. The legal efforts include New York’s Climate Change Superfund Act, which was blocked by a federal judge in August, and the Supreme Court’s pending Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County case. That case could determine whether state and local governments can pursue climate lawsuits against fossil fuel companies in state court. GAVIN NEWSOM'S 'HIDDEN CLIMATE TAX' HITTING AMERICANS NATIONWIDE, LAWMAKER WARNS Turner argued the lawsuits could also shift responsibility away from state and local leaders. "The concern about these superfund lawsuits is that they absolve elected leaders from doing the bad, boring part of governing, which is infrastructure and mitigation strategies," he said. Despite the rise in climate lawsuits and state "superfund" laws, Antoni said the issue has largely flown under the radar. articles.title: The future is here: What will a Millennial-Gen Z majority mean for America?
articles.summary: If there’s anything we should know about millennials and Gen Z, it’s that they hate being neatly fit into a box.
articles.body:
Everyone knows millennials and Gen Z as the young, internet-native faces of American society. But the stereotype of millennials as the part-time barista working at the local coffee shop is out of date: Millennials are now 30 to 45 years old, and the oldest Gen Zers are turning 30. These Americans are far more likely to be your knee surgeon today than they are your barista.

For decades, American politics has run on a binary that Baby Boomers built growing up amid the Cold War: communism versus capitalism, Team Red versus Team Blue. That framework fit a world with two clear sides. It fits a lot less neatly in 2026, when the free market and the internet age have handed us more choice than ever, from streaming platforms to ketchup brands.

If there’s anything we should know about millennials and Gen Z, it is that they hate being neatly fit into a box. This explains why people nowadays display significantly less brand loyalty than before when looking at consumer habits and trends. And this also explains why millennials and Gen Z identify as political independents at far higher rates than older Americans.

Data conducted by Gallup in January discovered that the majority of both Gen Z (56 percent) and millennials (54 percent) identify as political independents . This trend is likely to continue. Millennials and Gen Z combined already make up the largest voting bloc of the U.S. electorate . By 2028, Gen Z and millennials are projected to make up more than half of the electorate , and they will continue to dominate American politics for the next 20 years.

This demographic has experienced nothing but political gridlock, a failing immigration system and a national debt that continues to spiral out of control. Put simply, these voters have seen nothing but ineffective governance in Washington and are ready for something different.

This year’s election marks the first time where we’re seeing serious, viable independent candidates emerge to meet this growing demand driven by younger voters. In fact, this year is seeing one of the largest surges of independent candidates in recent memory , with dozens of candidates vying for public office across the country.

They offer genuine, nonpartisan, commonsense solutions that these voters are yearning for.

Millennials and Gen Z are not the future of American politics. They are the present. And this also means that independents are now a major, indisputable force that decides elections and shapes policy. From comprehensive immigration policy that secures our borders to AI/tech guardrails for children, there’s real potential for meaningful change that this demographic shift can usher in.

On immigration, younger voters reject the false choice between a wall and blanket amnesty; they want enforcement that actually works paired with legal pathways that exist, not a standoff that’s been stuck in place for 30 years. On AI and kids’ online safety, they’re equally unimpressed by regulate-everything and regulate-nothing. Having grown up as the first generations raised inside these platforms, they want guardrails that protect children without strangling the innovation that built the tools they use every day.

We should be encouraged that these generations are already thinking about one of the biggest of problems facing our country: Social Security insolvency. Writing for Fortune in August, Nick Lichtenberg noted that baby boomers are collecting 265 percent of what they paid into Social Security while millennials pick up the tab. Sixty-nine percent of Gen Z and 71 percent of millennials worry the program will run out before they ever see a dime .

Neither party has offered a credible fix; both sides seem intent on kicking the can down the road. Independent millennials and Gen Z Americans know that this can is going to eventually hit a wall, and they’ll be left to pick up the mess. You already see Sens. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) backing legislation to raise taxes instead of planning for lasting reform.

Millennials and Gen Z can back a solvency plan that is judged on whether it actually works for the generations footing the bill, not based on which party flinches first.

Social Security’s looming insolvency is just one of these major policy areas where millennials and Gen Z will lead. And consider the possibilities that independents represent because they’re not bound by either party’s outdated ideologies.

Remember, independents are not merely a trend driven by the historical unpopularity of the two parties. It’s a new era ushered in by the political maturation of the millennial and Gen Z generations.

Adam Brandon served as the president of FreedomWorks for more than a decade. Currently he is senior adviser at the Independent Center and author of “The Exhausted Majority: Building a Home for the Politically Homeless.”

articles.title: Trump revives rare budget maneuver to rescind $810M in congressionally approved funds
articles.summary: Trump used a pocket rescission to cancel $810 million in approved spending on refugee programs, diversity initiatives and migrant education.
articles.body: The Trump administration announced Friday that it was canceling $810 million in congressionally approved spending for programs serving illegal immigrants, diversity initiatives and other efforts the administration argued do not benefit American citizens. To claw back the funds, President Donald Trump used a "pocket rescission," a budget maneuver the executive branch contends is within its authority but that Congress and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) say exceeds the president's authority. The vast majority of the cuts, some $567 million, were aimed at Health and Human Services programs that provided funding to non-government organizations supporting refugees, asylees and other non-citizens. The White House is also seeking to rescind $25 million for education programs for migrant students, claiming they supported things such as "an LGBT youth summit" and "Therapy for Latinx workshops." TRUMP ADMIN AXES TIES TO DOZENS OF PROGRESSIVE GROUPS IN 'DIRECT OPPOSITION' TO MISSION: 'DECISIVE ACTION' Programs the administration labeled "Woke International Education" were also selected for $70 million in cuts. The White House said the funding supports bringing foreign students and faculty to the United States and, in some cases, has funded doctoral dissertations on "queer and trans community building in foreign countries." Other programs receiving the axe included a Justice Department office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, Housing and Urban Development Department counseling services, and a series of Health and Human Services grants the administration described as "outright harmful and blatantly ideological." The White House's announcement about the rescissions noted that several of the organizations are led by former officials in President Barack Obama's administration. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who faces a tough re-election campaign, condemned Trump's cuts and called it "the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse." WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD Under the most recent pocket rescission, the White House proposed canceling the funding near the end of the federal fiscal year on Sept. 30. Collins argued that this was intentional on the part of the Trump administration, because if the money remains unspent until Sept. 30, it expires before Congress' 45-day review period can be completed. On top of that, the House of Representatives will be out of session through the November election, making it essentially impossible for Congress to respond. "The independent Government Accountability Office has concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful and not permitted by the Impoundment Control Act," Collins said in a statement. "I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The OMB under Trump has argued that the Impoundment Control Act does not explicitly forbid the president from rescinding funds near the end of a fiscal year, according to a summary from the Congressional Research Service (CRS). OMB Director Russ Vought has repeatedly said the same. That same CRS summary said the GAO has likened pocket rescissions to a line-item veto, which would allow a president to strike portions of legislation without congressional approval — a power the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional. A year ago, Trump issued the first pocket rescission in nearly 50 years, seeking to cancel $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The Supreme Court declined to block the move, citing the president's authority over foreign affairs as it allowed litigation to continue. The last pocket rescission took place under former President Jimmy Carter, who proposed it well before the 45-day congressional review deadline.

articles.title: To make energy affordable again, end green mandates before the midterms
articles.summary: Democrats spent the summer talking a big game on “affordability,” but their energy approach raises prices across the board.
articles.body:
Amid all the talk about affordability, the Environmental Protection Agency’s repeal of Biden-era climate regulations is set to save Americans $310 billion by restoring cheap baseload power.

The final rule eliminates the EPA’s 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards. Those standards exceeded the agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act by requiring emissions-control technologies that do not actually exist yet — or in the EPA’s words, have not been “adequately demonstrated.” Biden’s rules forced power plants to retire early by setting standards they could never meet.

The 2024 rule also failed to account for the recent Supreme Court decision in West Virginia v. EPA , which barred the EPA from misusing the act to manipulate Americans’ energy choices and drive electricity prices up.

“The Obama and Biden administrations implemented a war on coal to destroy reliable and affordable energy,” said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin in a press statement . “The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on.” He said lower energy prices were “just the beginning.”

“Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices, and a more prosperous America.”

Democrats spent the summer talking a big game on “ affordability ,” but their energy approach raises prices across the board. Republicans should highlight that while the administration rolls back costly federal energy mandates that deep blue jurisdictions, such as Washington D.C., are imposing.

In the case of D.C., the energy mandate is so expensive that the city government exempted itself from following it. The District’s statue states that its new standard “shall not apply to electricity sold to the District of Columbia government, not including independent agencies, authorities, or instrumentalities.”

That hypocrisy needs more political attention. It creates a unique opportunity for President Trump and congressional Republicans to get a political win before the midterm. They can use constitutional authority to review D.C. Council legislation under the Home Rule Act to repeal these onerous mandates. The Constitution explicitly gives Congress “ exclusive Legislation ” over the District of Columbia, making this easy to do politically.

As a result of these so-called green mandates, D.C. electricity costs rose 66 percent — more than neighboring Maryland (50 percent) and Virginia (20 percent). The District’s renewable energy mandates have quadrupled compliance costs , from $65 million in 2020 to $272.6 million in 2025, for an average added annual burden of $775 per customer.

Why should every American pay a price that D.C.’s own government refuses to pay?

Energy prices are a function of public policy more than anything else. Examining the costs of energy throughout the country, it becomes easier to put a finger on who’s responsible for high prices: Blue states pay far more than red states do. According to the Institute for Energy Research’s 2025 Always on Energy Research report , U.S. electricity prices spiked 27 percent under the Biden administration, with the vast majority of this price increase affecting blue states.

Aggressive green energy targets, primarily in Democratic-leaning jurisdictions, caused power bills to soar in areas like the District, New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, Illinois, Delaware and Michigan, according to a recent study by the nation’s largest power grid operator . At the same time, states like North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana and West Virginia see no predicted price hike because they haven’t imposed green energy standards.

These mandates have already cost mostly blue state residents $17.8 billion in compliance costs over the last decade, with this number expected to significantly increase as more regulations come online. The average New Jerseyans spend 19.8 cents per kilowatt-hour of electricity, almost twice what the average West Virginian pays.

Those prices flatly contradict the “ affordability ” message that Democrats are running on. Republicans should highlight this massive discontinuity. If Washington wants to deliver on affordability, it can start by repealing energy mandates that are driving up electricity prices and making Americans pay more to keep the lights on.

Andrew Follett conducts research analysis for a nonprofit in the Washington, D.C. area.

Trump will fly to Knoxville Saturday morning to watch the Texas Longhorns, ranked…
articles.body:
President Trump will attend the University of Texas vs. University of Tennessee football game in Knoxville at noon on Saturday — an appearance coming ahead of senators’ last chance to pass the Protect College Sports Act before recessing into a lame-duck period.

Trump will fly to Knoxville Saturday morning to watch the Texas Longhorns, ranked number one in the AP Top 25 , face off against the Tennessee Volunteers, ranked 14th.

He is not expected to make any appearances on sports networks covering the game, as his fellow Republican, Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), did earlier this month — appearing on ESPN’s College Gameday to tout legislation.

It is not yet clear whether television news broadcasters will cover Trump’s travels to and from the game, as the president barred CNN from reporters on Air Force One and taking its turn as the trips designated pooler — a rotating group of journalists who cover the president when space is limited, sharing their information with other networks.

The White House has not yet named a replacement for CNN, who — along with MS NOW and Politico — have been locked in a legal battle with Trump after he attempted to ban them from his official residence.

Meanwhile, the Senate is preparing for its final week in session before a long recess will extend beyond election day in November. While some GOP candidates attempt to distance themselves from Trump’s policies after his approval rating hit a record low, Republicans in the Senate are preparing to make haste in passing legislation while they still hold a majority.

Following Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, D.C., it was announced that the U.S. and China agreed to cut tariffs on $30 billion worth of tariffs imported by one another, set up a channel for AI-related incidents and strengthen military crisis communications.

The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Wednesday that Washington and Beijing would extend their broader trade truce by two months, from Nov. 10 to Jan. 10, for a larger negotiation window.

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran’s 7-day plan to end war, expects bombing to resume post-midterms
articles.summary: President Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter a ceasefire and is considering renewed military strikes against the country after the midterm elections in November. Trump publicly responded to the proposal Saturday morning, telling reporters at the White House, “I’m rejecting their deal.” “They want to make a deal…
articles.body:
President Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and enter a ceasefire and is considering renewed military strikes against the country after the midterm elections in November.

Trump publicly responded to the proposal Saturday morning, telling reporters at the White House, “I’m rejecting their deal.”

“They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said. “You know you don’t read that, you don’t see that in the fake news. We’re winning tremendously. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait, massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait.”

“Last night we had 29 ships come out. They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine, I like making a deal, too, but that deal would not be acceptable,” the president continued.

Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strait and resume negotiations over its nuclear program.

According to a Wall Street Journal report citing U.S. officials, the president is skeptical over Iran’s ability to honor its end of the deal and told officials that he is contemplating resuming military strikes.

Tehran is seeking several concessions from the U.S. in return, including an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, waivers on sanctions targeting Iranian oil sales and a ceasefire that would extend to Lebanon, according to the Associated Press.

The president went on to tell reporters Saturday that Iran wants the ability to reopen the Strait of Hormuz “because they’re dying.”

“You know why they’re dying? Because they have no money coming in. Because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait,” he continued.

The president reiterated his demand that Tehran not obtain a nuclear weapon and put an end to its uranium enrichment efforts, posting “IRAN CAN NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!!!” on Truth Social Saturday.

Trump also posted an image Friday labeling the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy routes carrying roughly 20 percent of global oil supplies, the “Trump Strait.”

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that the decision to reopen the Strait of Hormuz “now rests with the United States,” after Tehran offered a plan that it says could restore normal shipping through the critical waterway within a week.

“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. “The choice now rests with the United States.”

Araghchi said Iran conveyed a “concrete seven-day plan” to the U.S. through mediator Qatar following talks between the two countries this week.

“The seven-day timeline starts as soon as the United States accepts this plan,” he said. “If they accept this plan tomorrow, the seven days will start from tomorrow.”

Araghchi said the U.S. could carry out the steps required under the proposal within four or five days.

He argued that some were already included in commitments Washington made in a memorandum of understanding signed in June between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire, which later collapsed.

articles.title: White House blocks CNN from covering Trump’s Tennessee trip
articles.summary: The White House on Friday night removed CNN from joining President Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday, where it was supposed to cover the president on behalf of major TV networks.
articles.body: The White House on Friday night removed CNN from joining President Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday, where it was supposed to cover the president on behalf of major TV networks. According to media guidance sent out by the White House on Friday night, CNN was removed from the list of outlets designated for pool coverage of Trump’s trip, in which he is set to attend a college football game in Knoxville. The pool is a rotating group of networks that share duties of filming the president both in Washington and on official trips. Other member networks — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in the pool this week after Trump banned CNN from serving as a member. CNN on Friday reported that it had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One on Saturday as part of its pool duties covering the president’s trip to the game between the University of Texas and the University of Tennessee. However in the president’s schedule released Friday night, CNN was not listed as a member of the pool and no other network was listed as replacing it. The move is the latest development in the White House’s attempt to restrict access by CNN and other outlets to cover the White House. The president last week had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House before a judge temporarily blocked that move Thursday and ordered the administration to restore their reporters’ credentials for 14 days. But while the order restored the outlets’ access to the White House, it didn’t explicitly require the administration to restore CNN’s participation in the television pool. The White House did not immediately return a request for comment.

articles.title: The October term heralds another ‘big year’ for the Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Supreme Court is set to begin a landmark term featuring significant cases regarding climate change, firearm regulations, religious discrimination in education, parental rights, and various constitutional amendments.
articles.body:
October is when hype meets reality. In baseball, the final teams are sorted out for the playoffs, and your football teams are well into the winnowing-out process for the Super Bowl. For court nerds, the start of the October term at the Supreme Court can have a similar dynamic, as long-watched cases finally come up for oral argument. Although the court continues to accept cases on a rolling basis, this term is looking like another blockbuster, with cases that range from climate change to gun rights to parental rights.

The odds of making the oral argument docket make the NFL season look like a walk in the park. After thousands of petitions, the Supreme Court accepts on average between 70-80 cases for the coveted “ writ of certiorari .” If you are a lower-court judge with an appealed case, this is one Super Bowl you would probably prefer to skip. The court generally reverses the cases it accepts for review. Last term, it had a 71 percent rejection rate, slightly up from the prior year.

This year already has a number of major cases that are likely to have transformative impacts on the law and society. Here are a few.

In Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, Boulder sued energy companies under theories of public and private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, and civil conspiracy, claiming that they knowingly contributed to climate change while misleading the public about its impacts.” The Colorado Supreme Court ruled for the city and the county in finding that such lawsuits are not barred by federal preemption. If the case is allowed to go forward, it would expose companies to potentially thousands of climate change lawsuits.

October is already shaping up as a major Second Amendment term. Democratic cities and states have been banning the AR-15, the most popular rifle in the U.S., and the 9mm semi-automatic handgun, the most popular handgun in the U.S. These cases out of the Seventh Circuit in Chicago (Viramontes v. Cook County) and the Second Circuit in New York (Grant v. Higgins) will likely give long-awaited clarity on these bans. They could potentially close off a major circumvention of prior rulings to achieve sweeping gun control policies.

In addition to these cases, the court is considering the possible review of Calce v. New York. In that case, the Second Circuit upheld a stun gun ban. The court previously sent back a similar case out of Massachusetts after the First Circuit ignored prior rulings. The court stressed that the fact that a weapon did not exist at the time of the ratification of the Second Amendment (such as “electric arms”) does not mean that they fall outside of the constitutional protections. The addition of Calce would make this one of the most momentous Second Amendment terms in history.

Parochial Schools and Religious Discrimination

The court will return to another parochial school controversy this term. In prior cases, the court has repeatedly stepped in to prevent states from discriminating against religious schools in voucher or subsidy programs. In St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, the Tenth Circuit upheld a Colorado provision that requires all preschools to agree not to discriminate on the “race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, income, or disability.” The Catholic challengers are arguing that the policy requires them to violate their religious values as a condition for participating in the preschool program and funding.

In International Partners for Ethical Care, Inc. v. Ferguson, Washington amended its laws to delay shelters in notifying parents of a runaway child who has “gender-affirming treatment” — the standard used for children in abusive homes. Instead, the Department of Children, Youth, and Families is first notified. The Ninth Circuit rejected parental claims raised in the case due to a lack of standing.

In Kian v. Florida, chiropractor Hamed Kian was convicted of five counts related to practicing with a suspended license. Pursuant to Florida law, he was tried by a six-person jury. Kian argues that the law violated his Sixth Amendment right to a jury of 12 members.

Some of us are watching a few other cases. Not surprisingly, my two favorites deal with the freedom of speech. The court has yet to decide whether to accept D.A. v. Tri-County Area Schools in which the Sixth Circuit upheld a school ban on high school students wearing “Let’s Go Brandon” sweatshirts. In the view of many of us in the free-speech community, the case is a major potential First Amendment ruling in the making.

Some of us also hope that the court will take up Tiny Zaps v. Traxler, which deals with a ban on tattoos on the face, neck, or head as well as a ban on tattoo parlors within 1,000 feet of churches, school, or playgrounds. The South Carolina Supreme Court upheld the ban, and it could allow the court to reinforce free-speech protections for “body art.”

The late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg once said, “It’s hard not to have a big year at the Supreme Court.” That is certainly true, but this term is already pretty big, and the court still has plenty of slots to fill before January.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor who teaches a class on the Constitution and the Supreme Court and is the best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution .”

articles.title: These were the hottest baby names in your state 50 years ago. Here’s where they rank now
articles.summary: If you are in your 50s, there’s a decent chance your name is one of three that topped the charts throughout the U.S. back in the 1970s.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – If you are in your 50s, there’s a decent chance your name is one of three that topped the charts throughout the U.S. back in the 1970s. You may, however, have a hard time finding at least two of those names on newly printed Social Security cards.

The administration responsible for those cards has been tallying the names dolled, and provides much of that data for your own perusal. The Social Security Administration annually reports the 100 most common names for boys and girls born each year. It’s because of this that we know there will soon be Liams and Olivias in kindergarten classes everywhere, if they aren’t already.

It’s also how we know that, if you turned 50 last year, your name is likely Jennifer or Michael or Jason.

We looked back at SSA data to find the top boy and girl names of 1975 (since we don’t yet know the top names of 2026, we had to use the most recent data set available, released last year, for a 50-year review).

Among girls born in 1975 (and any year between 1970 and 1984), the most popular name was Jennifer. While the most common name in each state can vary, Jennifer made a clean sweep in 1975, beating out any other girls’ name in all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

The battle was not as simple among newborn boys.

SSA data shows that while Michael was the most common name for boys born in 1975 (and from 1961 to 1998), it was only the top name in 35 states and the District of Columbia. Jason claimed the No. 1 spot in 15 other states.

The map below shows how Michael and Jason divided the country in 1975:

While Michael didn’t win it all in 1975, it does outrank Jason and Jennifer overall.

Since 1926, the SSA reports , there have been over 4.3 million Michaels born in the U.S. There may be even more, because “many people born before 1937 never applied for a Social Security card.”

Michael stands as the second-most-common name of those born in the U.S., coming in roughly 200,000 shy of James. Among boys, Jason is the 26th-most popular name since 1926, having been bestowed upon more than 1.05 million newborns.

Slightly more girls – about 1.47 million total – born since 1926 have been named Jennifer. It ranks No. 3 between Mary (2.8 million) and Patricia (1.5 million).

To find the last time either Jason or Jennifer ranked within the top 100 names for a state, you have to go back at least a few years.

Nexstar reviewed SSA baby name data following the fall of Jason and Jennifer. More specifically, we followed both names in each state from their spike in the 1970s until the last consecutive year they ranked within the top 100 names for boys and girls, respectively.

By around the early to mid-2000s, both names began ranking outside the top 100 names at the state level.

Jennifer hasn’t cracked a state’s top 100 since 2012, when it was No. 97 in California and Texas. Jason hasn’t been in a state’s top 100 since 2021, when it ranked at No. 72 in Maryland and No. 97 in Florida, based on a review of SSA data by Nexstar.

The interactive table below shows the last consecutive year in which Jennifer and Jason were among the 100 most popular girl and boy names, respectively, in your state.

While they’ve experienced a decline in popularity, Jason and Jennifer still remain among the most common baby names. According to the SSA , Jason was the 126th-most popular name for boys in 2025. Jennifer was the 586th most common among girls.

There may be a reason why names rapidly lose prevalence. Baby-naming consultant Colleen Slagen of NamingBebe.com told Nexstar in 2024 that she encourages people to avoid trendy names.

For comparison, Michael came in at No. 21 among boy names used last year, a spot on the charts that it hasn’t reached since 1938 .

You can use the Social Security Administration’s lookup tool to view how popular (or unpopular) your name or names you’re considering for your baby have been.

articles.title: Ending the roadless rule can help fight forest fires and improve wildlife access
articles.summary: Rescinding the roadless rule is not a threat to federal wilderness; it is a statement that we have enough already and that we need to manage it rather than let it burn.
articles.body:
On Aug. 23, the U.S. Forest Service announced that it is considering rescinding the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule . Across the country, newspapers ran stories saying this would open the wilderness to logging.

Supposedly, the rule was designed to preserve wilderness on federal lands. But it does not apply to places that feature “ sacred sites ” like Yellowstone or Yosemite or to congressionally designated wilderness areas like the iconic Aldo Leopold Wilderness in New Mexico or the Bob Marshall Wilderness in Montana.

As Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins explained , rescinding the rule would “restore authority to local forest managers who know the land best.”

Not surprisingly, the announcement drew an immediate backlash from environmentalists and Democrats. They claim this is a ploy to pad the pockets of timber companies at the expense of wilderness and that more roads will lead to more wildfires and degradation of wildlife habitat.

The data, however, support Rollins’s call for better fuel management. True, roughly 85 to 90 percent of wildfires are human-caused — sparked by vehicles, discarded cigarettes, campfires or power equipment. Areas with higher human traffic and vehicles experience a much higher concentration of fire starts.

But these are not the fires that spread rapidly and far. The primary drivers behind large and rapid spreading fires are related to inaccessibility.

Less access means delayed initial remediation, slower response times due to difficulties getting crews and equipment to the scene, heavier reliance on air suppression and small smoldering spots with more time to blow up into major conflagrations. There is also a lack of active management because roadless and wilderness areas undergo much less active logging, brush clearing and controlled burns, which reduces fuel for wildfires.

Alongside the fire debate is the question of what constitutes wilderness and how much is enough. In 1964, Congress passed the Wilderness Act famously describing a wilderness as a place “where the earth and its community of life are untrammeled by man, where man himself is a visitor who does not remain.” Untrammeled specifically means no roads, no ATVs or motorbikes and no motorized equipment, including chainsaws.

Initially, the act designated 9.1 million acres of federal land as wilderness, and since then we have added more than 100 million acres . Today wilderness defined by the act constitutes 18 percent of federal lands and 5 percent of the country .

Wilderness designated lands, however, are not the only roadless lands. In addition to the wilderness areas, there is another 58.2 million inventoried roadless acreage covered by the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule — approximately 30 percent of National Forest System lands.

Who uses those roadless areas? The best estimates we have of wilderness usage come from the period of 2000 to 2002, when there were about 8.8 million annual wilderness site visits and 600-700 million federal land recreation visits.

The reason for the difference is that most recreationists visiting the wilderness could care less about whether the land is untrammeled. They just want to get into the great outdoors without hiking miles carrying a heavy backpack. They would be happy to find remnants of an old goldmine or a prospector’s cabin and return to their VRBO in the comfort of their air-conditioned SUV.

Rescinding the roadless rule is not a threat to federal wilderness; it is a statement that we have enough already and that we need to manage it rather than let it burn.

Terry L. Anderson is the John and Jean DeNault Senior Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution.
